excerpts:
[ColombiaOne.com](https://colombiaone.com/) [News feed](https://colombiaone.com/newsletter-feed/ "View all posts in News feed") Keiko Fujimori Sworn in as Peru's First Elected Female President

# Keiko Fujimori Sworn in as Peru’s First Elected Female President

By [Josep Freixes](https://colombiaone.com/author/josep/)

\-

July 28, 2026

**Getting your Trinity Audio player ready...**

Keiko Fujimor was sworn in today as Peru’s first democratically elected female president, after narrowly defeating Roberto Sanchez Credit: Presidency of Peru.

Keiko Fujimori was sworn in as Peru’s president on Tuesday, becoming the first woman ever elected by popular vote to lead the country. Her inauguration marks the return of Fujimorismo to power 26 years after the collapse of the authoritarian regime led by her father, Alberto Fujimori, and opens a new chapter for a nation that has spent the past decade plagued by political instability and a constant turnover of presidents.
The Popular Force leader took office after one of the closest presidential elections in Peru’s recent history. Fujimori defeated left-wing candidate [Roberto Sanchez](https://colombiaone.com/2026/06/23/peru-roberto-sanchez-wont-recognize-keiko-fujimori-president/) by just 49,641 votes, a margin of slightly more than two-tenths of a percentage point. The razor-thin result triggered legal challenges, court appeals, and fraud allegations from the defeated camp before Peru’s National Jury of Elections officially certified the outcome.

The presidential inauguration, following the elections, takes place on July 28 under a constitutional mandate, coinciding with the anniversary of the country’s Proclamation of Independence, declared by Jose de San Martín in 1821. The date is a centerpiece of Peru’s Independence Day celebrations and was adopted through political and historical tradition to symbolize the beginning of each new presidential term.
## Keiko Fujimori sworn In as Peru’s first elected female president

Although [Dina Boluarte](https://colombiaone.com/2025/10/10/peru-removes-president-dina-boluarte-jose-jeri/) was the first woman to serve as Peru’s president, she assumed office through constitutional succession following the impeachment of Pedro Castillo in December 2022. [Keiko Fujimori](https://x.com/KeikoFujimori?lang=en) , by contrast, became the first woman to win the country’s highest office through a popular vote—an achievement widely regarded as historic in a nation where no female candidate had prevailed at the ballot box in more than two centuries of republican history.

The victory also capped Fujimori’s long electoral journey. After losing three presidential elections and enduring years of judicial investigations and intense political polarization, the conservative leader finally reached the presidency at the helm of a movement that continues to inspire both strong support and fierce opposition.
Her last name remains one of the most controversial in Peruvian politics. To her supporters, [Alberto Fujimori](https://colombiaone.com/2024/09/12/alberto-fujimori-peru-died/) was the president who defeated the Shining Path insurgency and stabilized the economy during the 1990s. However, his administration was also marked by serious human rights violations, corruption, authoritarianism, and a lengthy prison sentence for crimes against humanity. That legacy will inevitably shadow the new president’s administration.

Fujimori enters office facing the immediate challenge of governing a deeply polarized country. The narrow election result exposed a society almost evenly divided, with a large segment of the population continuing to question the political legitimacy of her government, even after electoral authorities rejected all legal challenges and officially declared her the winner.

Public security ranks among her most pressing priorities.
During the campaign, she pledged to intensify the fight against organized crime, crack down on extortion, and strengthen the state’s presence in response to rising violence affecting multiple regions of the country. She must also revive the economy, encourage private investment, and address the aftermath of recent natural disasters that have struck several parts of Peru.

Another major challenge will be ensuring institutional stability. Peru has had nine presidents in roughly a decade, a succession of leadership changes that has eroded public confidence in government institutions and disrupted policy continuity. The new president has pledged to complete her full term and restore governability, though she will have to do so in a fragmented political environment under constant public scrutiny.

Among the people who gathered outside the presidential palace in Lima, several were carrying photographs of Alberto Fujimori, the dictator and father of the current president.
Credit: Presidency of Peru.

## Colombia’s representation

The inauguration ceremony also produced a notable diplomatic development. Outgoing President [Gustavo Petro’s administration](https://colombiaone.com/2026/07/28/colombia-petro-administrations-worst-legacy-for-left/) did not send an official delegation to the inauguration of Peru’s new president, despite the event being one of Latin America’s most significant political milestones and taking place in a neighboring country.

The highest-ranking Colombian representation was led by Vice President-elect [Jose Manuel Restrepo](https://colombiaone.com/2026/07/15/colombia-restrepo-meets-with-secretary-rubio-in-washington/) , who attended on behalf of President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella. The delegation also included Foreign Minister-designate [Omar Bula](https://colombiaone.com/2026/07/08/colombia-de-la-espriella-names-next-foreign-minister/) and incoming Commerce Minister [Mauricio Gomez Amin](https://colombiaone.
com/2026/07/07/colombia-de-la-espriella-names-amin-beltran-and-gutierrez-to-cabinet/) , who represented [Colombia](https://colombiaone.com/colombia-news/ "Colombia news") ’s incoming administration in Lima.

During his visit, Restrepo met with Keiko Fujimori and emphasized the importance of strengthening bilateral ties between the two countries. The vice president-elect said it was an honor to accompany Peru’s new leader during a historic moment for the country and expressed the incoming Colombian government’s commitment to expanding political, economic, and trade cooperation with the new administration.

With her oath of office, Keiko Fujimori begins a presidency that will be closely watched both inside and outside Peru. Her supporters hope she can restore stability to a country battered by years of political turmoil, while her critics warn of the risks of a return to practices associated with Fujimorismo.

### Who is Dina Boluarte?

Dina Boluarte is a Peruvian politician who became the first woman president of Peru in December 2022 after Pres. Pedro Castillo was removed from office by Congress.

### Why was Dina Boluarte impeached?

Dina Boluarte was impeached on October 10, 2025, by the Peruvian Congress in a unanimous vote on the grounds of ‘permanent moral incapacity.’

### What was Dina Boluarte’s early life like?

Dina Boluarte grew up as the youngest of 14 children in a rural family in Chalhuanca, Peru.
She is fluent in Quechua and Spanish and initially studied nursing before pursuing law at San Martín de Porres University in Lima.

### How did Dina Boluarte enter politics?

Dina Boluarte entered politics relatively late, in her 50s. She joined the left-wing Free Peru party and ran unsuccessfully for mayor of Surquillo in 2018 and for a congressional seat in 2020.

### What led to Dina Boluarte becoming president?

Dina Boluarte became president after Pedro Castillo was removed from office by Congress on December 7, 2022. She was serving as his vice president at the time.

## Who is Dina Boluarte, Peru's first female president?

### Source: [CNN](https://www.cnnphilippines.com/world/2022/12/8/Peru-Dina-Boluarte-president-Pedro-Castillo-oust-Congress.html)

**(CNN)** — Dina Boluarte took office as the new President of Peru on Wednesday, after Congress ousted former president Pedro Castillo.

In this turbulent context, Boluarte, who until a few hours ago was the country's Vice President, took over as Castillo's successor after being sworn in before the plenary session of Congress on Wednesday afternoon.

She is the first female president in Peru's history, and the sixth Peruvian president in less than five years.

Boluarte's term will extend through July 2026.

LIMA, Peru—When Dina Boluarte was abruptly sworn in on Dec. 7, 2022, the fact that she was the first female president in Peru’s 201-year history was widely noted, yet barely explored by Peruvian media. Journalists had other things on their minds: Boluarte’s inauguration took place just hours after her predecessor Pedro Castillo was impeached for attempting to dissolve Congress and rule by decree, bringing down the curtain on a 17-month administration that had tipped the Andean republic into unremitting political instability and chaos.

Boluarte’s professional credentials as a lawyer felt like a qualitative leap forward for the presidency—regardless of the fact that she, like her predecessor, had never held public office before becoming vice president for the self-declared Marxist-Leninist Free Peru party in the June 2021 elections.

It looks increasingly inevitable that Peru’s first ever female president will face a similar fate to Castillo, the country’s first ever _campesino_ president (in Peru, the term means someone of indigenous ancestry who works the land), with a post-presidency dogged by legal problems and a potentially lengthy jail sentence.

At the time of writing, 48 Peruvians had been killed by security forces, some while protesting violently; some while demonstrating peacefully; and some who were just bystanders, including a medical intern treating an injured protester. Another dozen people died after protestors’ road blockades prevented them from receiving emergency medical treatment, and one police officer was found dead in a burnt-out patrol car.

In a [searing report](https://www.amnesty.

...

Boluarte, 60, who is bilingual in Spanish and the indigenous Quechua language, started her presidency relatively well. Indeed, in her inaugural address, she distanced herself from Castillo, referencing her “revulsion” at his [flagrant alleged graft](https://www.washingtonpost.com/world/2022/10/14/peru-president-castillo-corruption-complaint/) and condemning his “attempted coup.” Having been [expelled](https://larepublica.pe/politica/2022/01/23/dina-boluarte-comite-regional-de-lima-de-peru-libre-expulsa-a-vicepresidenta-por-falta-grave-vladimir-cerron) from the Free Peru party nearly a year earlier after openly disagreeing with the party’s more extreme politics—and after managing to stay clear of her predecessor’s endless corruption scandals—she had some credibility in the matter.

But her legacy, to the extent she has one, will remain inseparable from that of her predecessor.
This is not only a matter of the authoritarian excesses of her leadership over security forces, but also her emphasis on social conservatism, which has been one of the few areas of common ground between Free Peru’s presidential administrations and the hard-right congressional majority. Free Peru’s [campaign manifesto](https://perulibre.pe/wp-content/uploads/2020/03/ideario-peru-libre.pdf) has even been accused of advocating “ [machismo Leninism](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iUzma12c_Xs) ” for accusing the state of “subcontracting” its obligation to provide for the children of separated parents to absent fathers by requiring them to pay child support.

“It’s also a lesson learned,” Rivera Zea added. “What her presidency shows is that it is not enough to be a woman or speak Quechua if you don’t have that sensibility or identification with the historically excluded. She could have been a president who showed strength, wisdom, justice, and respect for human rights.
Instead, she has aligned herself with the worst in Peruvian politics.”

Far from being carried on the back of a feminist wave, Boluarte’s rise to power came at a particularly challenging time for gender rights in Peru, even as some other Latin American nations have been relaxing restrictions on abortion and increasingly tackling gender violence. Peru was already one of the most socially conservative societies in Latin America, with what are thought to be some of the highest rates of [sexual violence](https://www.worldbank.org/en/results/2021/04/13/combating-gender-based-violence-in-peru-increasing-awareness-and-resources-to-prevent-violence-against-women) in the region, and where abortion is only allowed in cases where the mother’s health is at risk.

It is unclear whether Boluarte has ever identified with the feminist movement, although she has shown an appreciation of gender issues.
“[Boluarte’s] not a feminist in the sense of a feminist activist,” Alexandra Ames, a political scientist at Lima’s University of the Pacific, said. “But she’s definitely a woman who feels that she has got ahead by working hard, harder than men would normally have to, and seems to have that awareness.”

While she was vice president, Boluarte also served as minister for development and social inclusion, a role that would normally have a strong gender component. During that time, gender rights came under a sustained assault from lawmakers, one that might have been met with effective resistance from a different executive.

Members of Congress sought to further restrict already highly limited abortion rights with a [blanket ban](https://www.infobae.com/america/peru/2022/11/16/comision-de-justicia-aprobo-proyecto-de-ley-que-obstaculiza-el-aborto-terapeutico/) , and [change the name](https://comunicaciones.congreso.gob.
pe/damos-cuenta/hoy-se-ve-cambio-de-denominacion-del-ministerio-de-la-mujer-por-ministerio-de-la-familia/) of the Ministry of Women to the Ministry for the Family—a switch that in Peru’s _machista_ society could have potentially life-and-death policy consequences for, for example, women facing abusive partners.

But the most damaging counter reform has been a new law allowing parents to [block classes](https://larepublica.pe/sociedad/2022/05/05/congreso-aprobo-dictamen-que-afecta-enfoque-de-genero-y-educacion-sexual-en-aulas-proyecto-de-ley) with a gender focus—or, as Peruvian conservatives call it, gender ideology.

First introduced to the national curriculum in 2004, gender focus concepts, which include sex education, were aimed at raising awareness among boys and girls of the harms caused by Peru’s patriarchal culture—everything from wage disparities to femicide. Conservatives, [often fundamentalist evangelical Christians](https://ojo-publico.

“She’s an Andean woman; she should have understood. Where’s the political skill, the ability to broker political compromise and then sell that to the population?”

Protesters are now demanding a constituent assembly to draft a new constitution capable of addressing stark economic injustices. However, a new constitution could also entrench gender inequality. Although there have been no polls on the issue of gender rights in a new constitution, surveys show that most voters want a conservative Magna Carta when it comes to social issues, [including](https://elcomercio.pe/opinion/editorial/editorial-un-problema-mayor-editorial-asamblea-constituyente-constitucion-iep-noticia/) prohibiting same-sex marriage and reinstating both compulsory military service and the death penalty.
